doc.title: Bill Allred interviewed by Monk Rowe, Orlando, Florida, February 24, 2017

title: Dixieland versus trad, and a high school band
summary: He distinguishes trad from Dixieland and recalls his high school tuba, accordion, trumpet and trombone band in Rock Island.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: I’ve often had a hard time describing to someone, or to my own self, the difference, if there is any, between Dixieland and trad and Chicago and classic.

You know it’s so complicated. I mean here I’ve played it for 50 some years. But it’s pretty much the same. Now the trad people, and I do the quotes, I mean they want to dwell really early on back to the early days of the New Orleans jazz. And Dixieland could encompass anything from the Dukes of Dixieland and Al Hirt and Pete Fountain, that sort of thing. I mean they stuck to their guns as far as the literature is concerned, as far as the tunes, except Al Hirt, he kind of branched out to the pop thing with all his little pop things, and they were tremendously successful. But I got weaned on Dixieland — when I was in high school we had a — I was just looking at the picture of it the other day, I can’t believe it — but we had a band consisting of tuba, accordion, trumpet and trombone. And a really, not really a jazz aficionado as far as the tuba player, but he was a good basic player. And the accordion player could play banjo as well. And we played at the basketball games in Rock Island, Illinois, in the ‘50 ‘1, ‘2, ‘3 I guess. And we played the fight songs and that, but we also played as much trad or Dixieland as we could get by with. And the band was pretty decent. And I still — just three of the guys out of our four are still around: me and Bob and Jim. So I got started on that right away.
